title: Sis
mood: A child who acts like a grown-up builds herself a friend. Then a new guard comes to the base.

hero.alt: In a dim lab a framed photo of two scientists holding a small girl stands on a desk, and beside it a white robot with rabbit ears rests on its stand, a small face on its screen.

segs.t: In the lab that same night, Chang’e had not slept. The photograph lay face up beside the empty pudding cup. Mr. Bunny hung over the desk with his screen turned down low.
She had been small enough to carry, then.
Terrinia’s research base, before the Academy.
The base’s two chief scientists had brought her there before she could walk properly. She remembered nothing from before. She never asked who her first parents were, and she never went looking.
The photograph was taken that first week, in the lab, with the two of them holding her up between them. They raised her as their daughter. They also made her their best student, because she was.
She called them Mom and Dad.

The base was all grown-ups and machines. Gray plates from dead Enders lay on the long benches, tagged and numbered. Her parents wanted to know how Enders worked. So far the plates had told them nothing.
Grown-ups could stay at the bench after dark. Children were sent to bed. So Chang’e was a grown-up.
One night she sat on a stool at the end of the bench with a tray of screws. She sorted them by size, faster than the researcher beside her, and told him so.
When the tray was done, she held it up and waited.

Her parents worked on with their backs to the room. Her father kept one hand in his pocket and turned a plate over with the other. A small blue vial was clipped at his chest. Her mother wrote with a mug in her free hand.
Neither of them turned.
“Bed,” said her mother, over the mug.
“I’m sorting.”
“Four hundred and twelve,” said her father, still facing the bench. He pushed his amber glasses up his nose. It was the count on her tray. He had been listening to the screws drop.
He slid a circuit board along the bench to her. That meant she could stay.
Chang’e lowered the tray and took the board.
Her mother cut a lab coat down to her size, so she could work without tripping. “Adult coats are inefficient on you,” she said.
Chang’e said it to a researcher the next day, about his own coat. Behind her round glasses, her mother laughed with her whole face, eyes shut.

blocks.caption: Chang’e’s father and mother, the base’s two chief scientists.

media.alt: A man in a white lab coat and amber glasses stands at a lab bench with his hands in his pockets, a small blue vial clipped to his chest, beside a framed family photo.
A woman in a white lab coat and round glasses laughs with her eyes shut, a mug in her hand, beside the same framed photo on the bench.

segs.t: Late nights ended with pudding, one cup each, eaten at the bench.
Medicine was a war. Once Chang’e had a cough, and her mother brought a cup of water with one pill beside it.
“I’ve reviewed the data,” said Chang’e. “I’ll recover on my own.”
Her mother leaned in the doorway with her mug and waited. She did not argue. She drank her tea.
Chang’e lasted until the mug was empty. Then she swallowed the pill. Her mother always won.
There were no other children on the base. Once Chang’e asked a researcher if he wanted to play.
“After this run,” he said.
The run took three days.
So she built a friend.

She worked on him in the evenings at the end of the bench, where her parents could see her if they turned around. He was a white ball with long ears. His face was a black screen, so he could make faces.
“What is it?” asked her father.
“A friend.”
He looked at it for a while. In the morning a better battery lay beside it.
Then the new guard came.

She was a soldier of the Shield, and young. Her gold hair was pulled back hard. A black patch covered her left eye, and a rifle hung on her back. At the gate she saluted Chang’e’s parents. Her mother held out a hand anyway, and the guard only looked at it.
“They’ve sent us a child,” a researcher muttered.
“She’s not a child,” whispered Chang’e, from behind her mother’s coat. “She has a rifle.”
The guard’s eye came down to her once. Then it went back to the gate.
Her name was Lesley. Chang’e read it off the duty board. Lesley walked the corridors at midnight and checked every door. The first night, Chang’e followed ten steps behind, in her coat.
“Bed,” said Lesley, without turning around.
“I’m doing rounds too.”
“Of what?”
“You.”
Lesley checked the next door.
“What happened to your eye?”
No answer. Lesley checked the door after that.
The next night Chang’e brought a lamp she had built to clip on a rifle. Lesley turned it over in her hand and gave it back.
“Not regulation.”
I’ll make it regulation,
thought Chang’e.
Two nights later she brought gloves with a heater in every finger. Lesley turned them over and gave them back.
“Not regulation.”
That night Chang’e sat on her stool with the gloves in her lap. Then she finished the friend.
She thought about what a friend should learn first. At the bench her parents worked with their backs to the room. Lesley walked away with her back to everyone.
“Front,” she told him. “That means come where I can see your face.”
He swung around in front of her face. His screen showed a smile with the eyes shut. It was her mother’s laugh, as near as a screen could get it.
She called him Mr. Bunny, for the ears. After that, when she was sad, he came around to the front without being told.
The next evening Chang’e stood in Lesley’s way at the lab door until Lesley stopped. Mr. Bunny rose from behind her back.
“Lesley, Lesley! Meet Mr. Bunny!” said Chang’e.
Lesley ducked down to look. Her hands came up and stopped halfway, open, holding nothing. She looked from Mr. Bunny to Chang’e and back, as if one of them might explain.

Chang’e beamed. Behind her, her mother laughed. Chang’e looked back. Both her parents had turned around on their stools. Beside the photograph on the bench, her father was trying not to laugh, and failing.

media.alt: A framed photo of two scientists holding a small girl stands on a bright lab bench as the view moves past it; a young woman with long gold hair bends down, gloved hands half raised, to a beaming pink-haired child who holds up a small white robot with rabbit ears; behind them a man and a woman in white coats watch.

segs.t: “He fetches,” said Chang’e. Mr. Bunny floated to her shoulder, and she leaned her head against him. “With Mr. Bunny and me, even 1 plus 1 is bigger than 2.”
Lesley poked him with one finger. His screen frowned.
“Don’t bully Mr. Bunny!” said Chang’e.
“Understood,” said Lesley. She took her finger back.
That night, over caramel pudding at the bench, her mother tapped her cup against Chang’e’s before she ate. Chang’e asked her a question.
“What do you call a girl who protects you? If she isn’t your mom.”
Her mother thought about it over her mug. “A big sister, I suppose.”
Under the bench, Chang’e tried it out on Mr. Bunny. “Big sister” took too long to say. It was inefficient.
“Big Sis,” she tried. That was better.
Then one shorter, for when there was no time. “Sis.”
His screen smiled.
At midnight Lesley walked the east corridor. The researchers stacked whatever they had no room for there, on steel shelving strapped along the wall.

Behind her came the small footsteps and the hum of the robot. They had followed her for weeks. When she stopped, they stopped. Lately the child even hid, as if waiting to be looked for. She did not look back.
At the corner her stride had gone short, so the small feet would not have to run. She had not decided that. She lengthened it again.
The child talked to a robot because there was nobody else. Lesley knew what that was. She had been the only child at the station.
Don’t know her,
she told herself.
Then it won’t matter.
She stopped at a door. Behind her, small shoes scuffed sideways. Something bumped the shelving.
The strap snapped.
Lesley turned. A rack taller than she was leaned out from the wall, over the white coat. She caught a fistful of the coat and pulled.
The rack came down where the child had been. Steel and glass hit the floor. The crash ran down the corridor and came back.
Then it was quiet. Dust turned in the light of the robot’s screen.
Two small arms wrapped around Lesley’s arm and held on. Two fists closed on the sleeve of her Shield coat.
“Sis!” said the child, into the sleeve.
Lesley went still.
It was her brother’s word.
Don’t know her,
she had told herself.
Too late for that.
Her free hand came up and stopped halfway, open, over the small head.
She did not answer. Somewhere in the heap, glass ticked as it settled. The child was shaking. Lesley could feel it through the sleeve.
Lesley did not pull her arm away. The small hands stayed where they were.
